meta.title: Who really said "I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Jackie Robinson wrote it in his 1972 autobiography I Never Had It Made, looking back on the 1947 World Series. Snopes rates it True.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Jackie Robinson, from I Never Had It Made (Putnam, 1972). The book uses a semicolon and opens the line with "As I write this twenty years later."

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1919–1972 · Brooklyn Dodgers infielder & civil rights activist
answer.sourceLine: Robinson wrote it in his 1972 autobiography I Never Had It Made, produced with the journalist Alfred Duckett and published by Putnam in New York. The book’s own text runs “As I write this twenty years later, I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world” — a semicolon where the circulating version puts a full stop.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: New York: Putnam, 1972 — Jackie Robinson with Alfred Duckett
Robinson looking back on the opening game of the 1947 World Series
Confirmed in the scanned first-edition text

source.excerpt: Today, as I look back on that opening game of my first World Series, I must tell you that it was Mr. Rickey’s drama and that I was only a principal actor. As I write this twenty years later, I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world. In 1972, in 1947, at my birth in 1919, I know that I never had it made.
trail: The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the scanned first edition gives the publisher and date as New York, Putnam, 1972, with Robinson and Alfred Duckett as authors: I never had it made ↗.

A full-text search of that scan — and of the 1995 Ecco Press edition — returns the sentence with a semicolon, “I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world”: Open Library search inside ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced Quotes section, crediting I Never Had It Made (1972) as told to Alfred Duckett, excerpted in Newsday on 5 November 1972.
Snopes ↗ rated the attribution True in 2016, printing the surrounding pages and citing Robinson and Duckett, I Never Had It Made (New York: Putnam, 1972).
source.cutTag: the scene at Yankee Stadium precedes this
source.excerptNote: Note the semicolon after “flag” and the opening clause “As I write this twenty years later” — both are usually lost when the line is shared.

author.name: Jackie Robinson
author.heading: Who was Jackie Robinson?
author.metaLine: 1919–1972 · Brooklyn Dodgers infielder & civil rights activist
author.bio: Jack Roosevelt Robinson was the first African American to play in Major League Baseball in the modern era, starting at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers on 15 April 1947 and ending decades of segregation in the professional game. He was far more than a ballplayer: he edited Our Sports magazine, publicly attacked segregation in restaurants and hotels, became the first Black vice president of a major American corporation at Chock full o’Nuts, and wrote to presidents about the pace of civil rights. He died in 1972 at the age of 53, the same year his autobiography appeared.

misattribution.heading: What gets changed
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Robinson. What travels badly is the punctuation, one missing clause, and the impression that he was describing something he did on a ballfield.

items.why: Almost every reposting breaks the line into three sentences: “I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world.” Even Wikiquote ↗ prints the full-stop form. Full-text search of the scanned 1972 edition returns a semicolon: “I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world.”

The sentence in the book begins “As I write this twenty years later” — the clause that marks it as a retrospective written for the memoir. Snopes reproduces the passage with that opening intact in its fact check ↗.

Some databases render the opening as “I cannot stand and sing the national anthem” — see LibQuotes ↗. The book says simply “the anthem” in that sentence, though “the national anthem” appears twice in the scene just before it.

The line is often passed along as though Robinson had refused to stand during his playing days. He did not write it then. It closes a scene set at the opening game of the 1947 World Series — a moment he says “should have been a glorious moment for me” — written up for a book published in 1972, as reprinted by Snopes ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Robinson wrote every word of it. If you want his punctuation rather than the internet’s, it is “I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world” — confirmed inside the scanned Putnam first edition via Open Library’s search-inside index ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: I Never Had It Made came out in 1972, the year Robinson died at 53. The passage that carries this line is not an outburst; it is the deliberate close of a long look back at Yankee Stadium on the opening day of the 1947 World Series — the band, the flag, and a man who calls himself “a symbolic hero to my people” and then refuses to let the scene be triumphant. The point is not that he walked out on the anthem in 1947. The point is what a quarter-century of being the experiment had taught him by the time he sat down to write.

The sentence had a loud second life in 2016, when it began circulating during the debate over athletes kneeling during the anthem. Both Snopes ↗ and Truth or Fiction ↗ published verification pieces on the same day — 30 August 2016 — and both confirmed the words as Robinson’s own.
detailsBody: The first edition is I Never Had It Made (New York: Putnam, 1972), credited to Jackie Robinson with Alfred Duckett; the Internet Archive’s catalogue record for its scan lists exactly that publisher and year.
The book stayed in print. The Internet Archive also holds a 1995 edition published by Ecco Press of Hopewell, New Jersey, under the title I never had it made: an autobiography.
Wikiquote cites the line to the 1972 book and to a newspaper excerpt, “Why ‘I Never Had It Made’: Jackie Robinson’s Own Story,” published in Newsday on 5 November 1972.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section carries "I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag. I know that I am a black man in a white world." credited to I Never Had It Made (1972) as told to Alfred Duckett, excerpted in Newsday (November 5, 1972).

Snopes rates the claim that Jackie Robinson said "I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world" as True, reprints the surrounding passage, and cites Robinson and Duckett, I Never Had It Made (New York: Putnam, 1972).

Truth or Fiction (30 August 2016) confirms Robinson wrote "As I write this twenty years later, I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world" in I Never Had It Made, and links it to the 2016 anthem debate.
The Internet Archive holds a scan of I never had it made, publisher "New York, Putnam", date 1972, creators Robinson, Jackie, 1919-1972 and Duckett, Alfred.

Open Library's search-inside index returns the phrase "I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world" inside the scanned editions ineverhaditmade00robi (Putnam, 1972) and ineverhaditmadea0000robi (Ecco Press, 1995).

NBC Sports reproduces the full passage from I Never Had It Made (1972), including "There I was, the black grandson of a slave... It should have been a glorious moment for me... As I write this twenty years later, I cannot stand and sing the anthem."

NBC Sports notes Robinson's activism beyond 15 April 1947: editing Our Sports magazine, criticising segregation at restaurants and hotels, and becoming the first Black vice president of an American corporation at Chock full o'Nuts.

LibQuotes renders the line as "I cannot stand and sing the national anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world," sourced to I Never Had It Made (1972), and gives Robinson's dates as 31 January 1919 - 24 October 1972 (aged 53).

The Saturday Evening Post essay quotes "I cannot stand and sing the anthem. I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world" from I Never Had It Made (1972) and places it alongside Robinson's 1944 Fort Hood court-martial and wider anti-racist activism.

Truthout reproduces the passage including "Today as I look back on that opening game of my first world series... As I write this twenty years later, I cannot stand and sing the anthem, I cannot salute the flag; I know that I am a black man in a white world." from Robinson's 1972 autobiography.

Beyond Chron quotes the passage beginning "I guess if I could choose one of the most important moments in my life, I would go back to 1947, in the Yankee Stadium in New York City. It was the opening day of the World Series..." through "...I know that I never had it made."

Wikipedia records that Jack Roosevelt Robinson was the first African American to play in Major League Baseball in the modern era and broke the color line starting at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers on April 15, 1947.
Open Library's work record OL15837204W is I Never Had It Made by Jackie Robinson and Alfred Duckett, covering the Putnam 1972 and Ecco Press 1995 editions.
